The cliffs above the camp, slick with rain.
The other children used ropes. You used the storm: the charge in your hands held you to the iron in the rock.
"Lightning does not fall, Kael. It CLIMBS. Watch it sometime."
The harbour in spring, the ice breaking up under your feet.
You did not stop running. You sang the next step into being, and the next, and the next.
The sea never caught you. It only ever held you up.
The First Hunt
Grass to the horizon, bending under a wind that smells of rain.
A boy lies flat in it beside a wolf made of stormlight. Neither of them breathes.
The herd breaks. The wolf goes left. The boy goes right. They have never needed words.
A horn sounds from the camp. Someone is calling the hunters home by name.
The Clap Before the Rain
Night on the steppe. Raiders at the edge of the firelight.
The pack-mother strikes her palms together once - and the sky answers through her.
"You do not need teeth for every fight, Fenn. Sometimes you only need to be LOUD."
The Wolf That Stayed
The sky over the steppe tore open. Violet light. The herd scattering.
You whistled, and the storm-wolf came, and stood between the tear and the camp.
It did not run when you fell. It is still out there. It has been waiting for the whistle.
Claws on Stone
The storm-wolf went up the cliff face as if it were level ground.
You followed with your hands crackling, each grip a small bite of lightning in the rock.
At the top it looked back at you. That was the day it stopped being a hunt and became a pack.
The Warden of the Stones
Mountains like the knuckles of the world, and below them a ring of standing stones.
A giant of a man walks the ring at dusk, laying one hand on each stone. Each one hums back.
Children follow him, daring each other to touch his shadow.
One of them shouts a name, and he turns, slow as weather, and smiles.
What the Ground Holds
A rockslide above the high pasture. Herders frozen on the path.
You did not run. You knelt, and put both fists to the ground, and ASKED.
The slide parted around them like a river round a stone.
The Dragon Under the Ring
The sky tore over the standing stones. Violet light pulled at the ring itself.
You called down - past the roots, past the bedrock - to the old thing asleep under the mountain.
It rose, and held the stones in place while everyone ran. Then the ground closed over you both.
You never climbed the mountain. You asked it, and it made room for your hands.
Every hold was there before you reached for it.
"The stone remembers its warden, Brakk. Wherever the sky drops you, put your hand on a wall."
The Ridge Runner
A ridge above the steppe where the wind never stops.
A boy runs along it with his arms out, scarf snapping behind him like a flag.
He jumps a gap between two rocks that no one should be able to jump. The wind holds him a moment too long.
Below, the herders shout his name - half scolding, half laughing.
The kite-fliers of the ridge did not pull their kites up. They asked the air to rise.
You asked once, as a joke, standing under your little sister.
She went up laughing. It took the whole camp to talk her down.
The Eye of It
The sky tore, and the wind went mad trying to fill the hole.
You ran INTO it. Round and round the tear, faster, until the air ran with you.
A wall of wind stood between the camp and the wound. You were the middle of it.
Holding On
The wind taught you to let go. The cliffs taught you the other thing.
A gust pinned you to the rock face once, flat as a leaf, and held you there until you found the handholds.
"See?" it seemed to say. "I can do gentle, too."
The Fireworks Girl
A storm-season festival on the steppe. Every clan has brought something to throw at the sky.
A girl with burnt eyebrows sets down a tube she built herself and tells everyone to stand further back. Further.
The sky turns gold from one horizon to the other. The thunder itself goes quiet to watch.
Then the whole camp is shouting one name.
Patience, With a Fuse
Wolves at the herd, every night for a week.
You did not chase them. You buried six clay pots along their trail and went to bed.
In the morning there were six craters, and no more wolves.
The Big One
The sky tore. Everyone ran from it. You ran to your workshop.
Everything you had ever built went into one casing, with the shortest fuse you ever cut.
You aimed it at the hole in the sky. It did not close the hole. But it made the hole FLINCH.
Climbing Irons
You hated heights. So you built something about it.
Charged grips, one for each hand, that bit into iron-stone and would not let go until you told them to.
"It is not climbing," you told everyone. "It is controlled falling. Upward."
The High Eyrie
A tower of ice above a frozen harbour. Falcons the colour of snow wheel around it.
A woman stands on the highest ledge with one arm raised. She does not call. She waits.
The largest bird folds out of the sky and settles on her glove like a held breath.
Far below, a child on the harbour ice waves both arms and shouts up at her.
A blizzard on the harbour road. Wolves circling a sled.
You did not raise your voice. You breathed out, once, and the storm held its breath with you.
Everything within ten paces stopped: the snow, the wolves, the fear.
The Bird That Came Back
Falling. Wind. The sky a shrinking coin above you.
You raised your arm out of habit - and something answered. Wings of new ice, shaped from the air itself.
It was never one bird. It was the cold, choosing to come when you called.
Steps on Air
The falcons never taught you to fly. They taught you something smaller.
That the air will take your weight for exactly one heartbeat, if you ask it politely and do not look down.
One heartbeat is enough, if you take them one after another.
The Blue Forge
A harbour locked in ice, and at its heart a forge that burns blue.
A girl feeds it with her bare hands. The ice-smiths sing the blades; she is the reason the song has heat.
Sparks climb her arms like they are glad to see her.
The old smith laughs and calls her in from the cold.
Banked Coals
The forge at midnight. The smiths asleep. Something clawing at the door from outside.
You did not throw the fire. You let it out, all round you, like opening your arms.
"A flame that only goes forward is a spear, child. A hearth goes EVERYWHERE."
The Sun in the Lab
White walls. Straps. A voice counting down to another test.
They wanted to know how hot you could burn. So you showed them.
For one breath there was a second sun in Sector 4. Then there was no Sector 4.
Walking on Heat
The harbour children ran on the sea-ice, freezing each step ahead of them.
You were the forge-girl. You were not supposed to be able to.
You learned anyway. Fire is only the cold, given somewhere to go.
The Ember-Carrier
A harbour of ice, and under it, far down, a red glow where the mountain breathes.
A woman walks up out of the deep vents with her hands cupped, carrying something that lights her face from below.
The smiths make way for her. The forge cannot be lit without what she brings.
A child tugs her sleeve and says her name like a question.
Where the Ground is Thin
The harbour ice groaned one winter, and a raiding ship came in over it.
You stamped once. The sea-floor remembered it was a mountain.
A column of red came up through the ice between the ship and the shore, and stood there, and dared them.
The Tide of Stone
White walls. A cradle of pipes. Cold going in, heat going out, for days without number.
You let it build. You were patient. Mountains are patient.
When it finally moved, it went across the floor like a tide, and nothing in the room was the shape it had been.
The children of the harbour ran on ice they made themselves, a step at a time.
You could not make ice. But you learned what the forge-masters knew:
even molten stone will hold you up, if you ask it to set at exactly the right moment.
The Lamplighter
A frozen harbour at dusk. One by one, lamps come alight along the sea wall.
Nobody sees who lights them. There is only a scarf, red against the snow, already at the next lamp.
The harbour sleeps safe because something it never sees walks the wall all night.
An old watchman raises his cup to the dark and says a name, fondly.
Behind You
A cutpurse on the harbour stair, running, laughing, certain he was clear.
He looked back to see how far behind you were.
You were not behind him.
The Long Cut
White light. A room with no shadows in it, built that way on purpose.
They forgot the one under the table.
You crossed the room in a single line. Everything on that line had been standing. Then it was not.
Stepping Stones
The harbour children ran on ice they froze under their own feet.
You could never do it their way. You did it yours:
a foot placed on a falling snowflake, a rooftop, a held breath - anything, for exactly as long as it was there.
